title: Introducing the EEF Guide to Inclusive Teaching
author: Education Endowment Foundation
summary: The Education Endowment Foundation's Evidence Edit newsletter introduces the newly launched EEF Guide to Inclusive Teaching, presenting it as a practical, evidence-informed resource to help all pupils participate and succeed in school. The guide is organized around a two-part model: universal approaches (evidence-informed practices that strengthen everyday teaching and are particularly important for pupils with additional needs) and adaptations and additional support (classroom adjustments, small-group teaching, one-to-one support, and targeted interventions deployed strategically). The newsletter emphasizes that these two elements are not sequential — strong universal teaching is the foundation, and adaptations build upon it — and that they work together rather than as separate tracks. The EEF also released accompanying interactive, scenario-based training resources to help teachers develop their inclusive teaching practice in realistic classroom contexts. The framing throughout is that inclusive teaching is not a specialist concern but a quality-of-teaching concern: every teacher benefits from understanding these approaches because they strengthen instruction for all students while specifically addressing the barriers that students with additional needs face.
points: The EEF's two-part model reframes inclusive teaching as a quality-of-teaching question for all classrooms, not a specialist concern limited to SEND provision — the universal approaches benefit every student.
Universal approaches form the foundation; adaptations and additional support are deployed on top of that foundation, meaning no additional support can compensate for weak universal teaching.

The interactive scenario-based training materials signal a shift in how the EEF expects teachers to develop inclusive practice: not through reading the guidance but through applying it in simulated classroom decision-making contexts.

The guide's emphasis that universal approaches are 'particularly important' for pupils with additional needs — not merely helpful — has significant implications for how schools should think about whole-class instruction versus pull-out support.

The launch reflects the EEF's broader evidence base showing that high-quality teaching for all (not specialist intervention alone) is the most powerful lever for improving outcomes for disadvantaged and vulnerable students.
quotes: Read more ( I The two-part model ( The guide introduces a practical two-part framework: * Universal approaches – evidence-informed classroom practices that benefit every pupil and are particularly important for pupils with additional needs. * Adaptations and additional support – classroom adaptations, small-group teaching, one-to-one support and targeted interventions used where needed to enable pupils to access high-quality teaching.

Strengthening and sustaining these approaches is likely to benefit all pupils and can reduce, though not remove, the need for additional support. Drawing on the best available evidence, the guide highlights five areas of universal practice: * Explicit instruction: clear, well-sequenced teaching that supports all pupils to access new learning.

* Positive relationships: predictable, supportive interactions that help pupils feel safe and ready to learn. * Calm classroom environments: routines and settings that reduce unnecessary barriers to participation.

But it is important to recognise that adaptations and additional support can be effective or ineffective, and that ineffective support or adaptation can hinder learning. For example, oversimplifying tasks in ways that reduce pupils' thinking can limit learning.

Explore effective and ineffective adaptations ( I Inclusive teaching myth-busting ( We address some of the most common misconceptions about inclusive teaching: * Inclusive teaching is all about what schools do differently for pupils with additional needs. * The more adaptations teachers make, the more pupils will learn.

* Teachers need specialist expertise before they can effectively support pupils with additional needs. By addressing these misconceptions directly, the guide encourages schools to focus on evidence-informed approaches that strengthen teaching for all pupils while providing effective additional support where needed.
